senses: to consider, be of the opinion
la:verb:arbitror.html:
arbĭtror (
act. arbitro, v.infra; arch. inf. arbitrarier, ), ātus, 1, v. dep.
arbiter
.
In gen., to be a hearer or beholder of something (v. arbiter, I.), to observe, perceive, hear, etc. (in this sense only ante- and post-class.): dicta alicujus,; ; ; , p. 138, 23; 7 init.: domus attiguae fortunas arbitraturus,, p. 148, 8.—Hence of the mind, to examine, consider, weigh: diligentius carmina Empedoclis,.—
Esp.
T. t. of judic. lang. (cf. arbiter, II.), to make a decision, give judgment or sentence: si in eo, quod utroque praesente arbitratus est, arbitrio paritum non esset,; .—Hence, fidem alicui arbitrari, to adjudge, i. e. to give, credit to one, to put faith in, .—Of witnesses, as t. t., to testify, to declare or announce, give evidence: qui testimonium diceret, ut arbitrari se diceret, etiam quod ipse vidisset,: qui primum

illud verbum consideratissimum nostrae consuetudinis arbitror, quo nos etiam tunc utimur, cum ea dicimus jurati, quae comperta habemus, quae ipsi vidimus, ex toto testimonio suo sustulit, atque omnia se scire dixit, : mortuum inde arbitrari,; .—

In gen., to be of the opinion, to believe, consider as, = νομίζω (most freq. in prose; a favorite word with Cic.): Bene facta male locata male facta arbitror, Enn. ap. : gratum arbitratur esse id a vobis sibi,: nefas esse arbitrari Gracchos laudare,: Falsum arbitror radices arborum vetustate minui,: Justum autem arbitror suscitarc vos, Pet. 1, 13: scelestissimum te arbitror,: arbitraris me inimicum tuum,; : si hoc minus ad officium tuum pertinere arbitrabere, suscipiam partes, quas alienas esse arbitrabar,: ut in ceteris artibus ... similiter arbitror in hac ratione dicendi etc.,; ; ; ; ; ; ; : tamen, ut arbitror, auctoritate advocatorum adducti in veritate manserunt,; so ; ; : ut ego arbitror,; : sicut arbitror,: ego quod ad me attinet (itemque arbitror ceteros) idcirco taceo, quod, etc.,: arbitratus id bellum celeriter confici posse,: Jugurtham esse arbitrati cum magno gaudio obvii procedunt,thinking it to be Jugurtha,: non satis tuta eadem loca sibi arbitratus,; so —
To think, suppose, as opp. to knowing: Arbitror: Certum non scimus,: si hunc noris satis, Non ita arbitrere,: De. Sanumne credis te esse? Mi. Equidem arbitror, : Quid consilii ceperis, quem nostrūm ignorare arbitraris?; : arbitrantur se posse fugere,; .!*?
Act. form arbĭtro, āre: te si arbitrarem dignum,: Probiores credo arbitrabunt,. —
Arbitror in pass. signif.: continuo arbitretur (i. e. eligatur, quaeratur) uxor filio tuo,: cum ipse praedonum socius arbitraretur,; ; ; cf. Zumpt ad l. l.: quaestio in utramque partem a prudentibus viris arbitrata, i. e. judicata,: sumptus funeris arbitrantur pro facultatibus defuncti,are estimated,; so ; : ex scriptis eorum, qui veri arbitrantur, ὑπολαμβάνονται, Cael. ap. P.

la:noun:arbitratus.html:
arbī^trātus, ūs, m.
arbitror
.
The judgment (as will, not as opinion; accordingly = voluntas, not = sententia), freewill, inclination, pleasure, wish, choice, decision (class.; cf. : hic allegatus et hic arbitratus pro allegatione proque arbitratione dicuntur. Quā ratione servatā arbitratu et allegatu meo dicimus, which latter expression is most freq. used): viri boni arbitratu resolvetur,; so : arbitratu domini,: nunc quidem meo arbitratu loquar libere, quae volam et quae lubebit,: Vapulabis meo arbitratu et novorum aedilium,; so ; ; ; ; : tuus arbitratus sit: comburas, si velis,; so : Er. Agedum, excutedum pallium. St. Tuo arbitratu, ; ; ; ; ; : quas (sententias) exposui arbitratu meo,: ut id meo arbitratu facerem,, and ; : tuo vero id quidem arbitratu,; so ; : suo arbitratu,: ejus arbitratu fieri,: arbitratu suo,: Tr. Quoius arbitratu nos vis facere? Gr. Viduli arbitratu, ; : senatūs arbitratu,; so .—
Direction, guidance: considerare oportet, cujus arbitratu sit educatus,; so .

senses: arbitrator, arbiter (having a wider power than a iūdex)
la:noun:arbiter.html:
arbĭter, tri, m.
ar = ad (v. ad init.) and bito = eo
, orig.,
one that goes to something in order to see or hear it; hence, a spectator, beholder, hearer, an eye-witness, a witness (class. through all periods; used several times by Plaut., but only twice by Ter.; syn.: testis, speculator, conscius).
In gen.: aequi et justi hic eritis omnes arbitri,: mi quidem jam arbitri vicini sunt, meae quid fiat domi, Ita per impluvium introspectant,: ne arbitri dicta nostra arbitrari (i. e. speculari, v. arbitror) queant,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : aut desine aut cedo quemvis arbitrum,: quis est decisionis arbiter?: ab arbitris remoto loco,: remotis arbitris,after the removal of,: omnibus arbitris procul amotis, Corte: arbitros eicit,: remotis arbitris,: sine arbitro,: absque arbitris,: loca abdita et ab arbitris libera, B; : secretorum omnium arbiter, i. e. conscius,: procul est, ait, arbiter omnis, (cf. : conscius omnis abest).—
Esp.
In judic. lang., t. t., prop., he that is appointed to inquire into a cause (cf. adire hiberna, , and intervenio) and settle it; hence, an umpire, arbiter, a judge, in an actio bonae fidei (i. e. who decides acc. to equity, while the judex decides acc. to laws), (cf. Zimmern, Rechtsgesch. 3 B, § 8; 3 B, § 42; 3 B, § 60 sq., and the jurists there cited).— So in the fragments of the Twelve Tables: JVDICI. ARBITROVE. REOVE. DIES. DIFFISVS. ESTO., ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. reus, p. 227 Müll.: PraeTOR. ARBITROS. TRES. DATO. ap. Fest. s. v. vindiciae, p. 376 Müll., and the ancient judicial formula: P. J. A. V. P. V. D., i. e. PRAETOREM JVDICEM ARBITRVMVE POSTVLO VTI DET, P.: ibo ad arbitrum,; so : Vicini nostri hic ambigunt de finibus: Me cepere arbitrum, (arbiter dabatur his, qui de finibus regendis ambigerent, Don.); so, arbiter Nolanis de finibus a senatu datus,.—Of the Hebrew judges: subjacebit damno, quantum arbitri judicaverint,.—Hence, trop.: Taurus immensus ipse et innumerarum gentium arbiter,that sets boundaries to numerous tribes,: arbitrum familiae herciscundae postulavit,: arbitrum illum adegit (i. e. ad arbitrum illum egit; cf. adigo),: quis in hanc rem fuit arbiter?.—In the time of Cicero, when, acc. to the Lex Aebutia, the decisions were given in definite formulae of the praetor, the formal distinction between judex and arbiter disappeared, —
Transf. from the sphere of judicial proceedings, a judge, an arbitrator, umpire, in gen.: arbiter inter antiquam Academiam et Zenonem. : Judicet Dominus, arbiter hujus diei, inter etc.,.—So of Paris: arbiter formae,: pugnae, the judge, umpire of the contest, ὁ βραβευτής, : favor arbiter coronae,which adjudged the prize of victory,.—
He that rules over, governs, or manages something, a lord, ruler, master (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; syn.: rex, dominus): arbiter imperii (Augustus), : armorum (Mars),: bibendi, (cf. : nec regna vini sortiere talis, and in Gr. βασιλεὺς τοῦ συμποσίου): quo (sc. Noto) non arbiter Hadriae Major,who rules over the sea,: arbiter Eurystheus irae Junonis iniquae,i. e. the executor, fulfiller of her wrath,—In prose, : regni,, where Halm reads arbitrium: rerum,: di potentium populorum arbitri,: (JOVI) RERVM RECTORI FATORVMQVE ARBITRO, et saep.

senses: something made from a tree, of wood
the polypus (imagined to have arms like the branches of a tree)
la:noun:arbor.html:
arbor (arbŏs, ; Lachm.; ; (but Merk.
arbor, in both places); ; ; ; ; Rib. al.: acc. arbosem, Paul. ex Müll.), ŏris, f. (m., INTER DVOS ARBORES, Inscr. Lyon, I. 27) [v. arduus].
A tree.
In gen.: arbores serere, to plant, Caecil. Stat. ap. ; : poni,: arbos se sustulit,: arbores putare,: arbores frondescere, Enn. ap. : arboribus frondes redeunt,: arbos silvestris,: ramosa, [1096]: umbrosa,; so : ingens,: alta,: summa,; so : patula,: fertilis,: in quibus (arboribus) non truncus, non rami, non folia sunt,: sub ramis arboris altae,, and : arborum rami,: arbor nuda sine frondibus,; : arborum cortices,: arbores ab radicibus subruere,; ; : quarum (arborum) baca,: jacent sua quāque sub arbore poma,; : fructus arborum,; .—
Spec. with gen. of species: alni, the alder-tree, Varr. R. R. 1, 7, 7: fici,the fig-tree,; : arbores ficorum,: arbor ficus (nom.), : abietis arbores,fir trees,: arbor palmae,the palm-tree,: cupressūs,the cypress,: arbor sycomorus,a sycamore,; so, arbor morus,: arbores olivarum,olive trees,.—Poet.: Jovis,the oak-tree,: Phoebi,the laurel-tree, (cf. : Apollinea laurus): Palladis,the olive-tree,: arbor Herculea,the poplar, (cf.: Arborum genera numinibus suis dicata perpetuo servantur, ut Jovi aesculus, Apollini laurus, Minervae olea, Veneri myrtus, Herculi populus,; ) al.—
Meton.
Things made of wood (cf.: Mille sunt usus earum (arborum), sine quīs vita degi non possit. Arbore sulcamus, maria terrasque admovemus; arbore exaedificamus tecta; arborea et simulacra numinum fuere etc.,).
A mast.
With mali: adversique infigitur arbore mali,.—
Without mali, ; ; . 2, t. 3.—
The lever or bar of a press, press-beam, ; ; .—
An oar: centenāque arbore fluctum Verberat adsurgens,.—
A ship: Phrixeam petiit Pelias arbor ovem,the ship Argo,.—
The shaft of a javelin, a javelin, .—
Euphemist.: arbor infelix, a gallows, gibbet: caput obnubito, arbori infelici suspendito,; ; cf. (Niebuhr, Röm. Gesch. I. § 365, compares the words of the Fries. law: am argen vordern Baum henken; cf. in Engl. to hang on the accursed tree).—
The fabulous polypus, which was fancied to have arms like the branches of a tree: In Gaditano Oceano arbor in tantum vastis dispansa armis, ut fretum numquam intrāsse credatur,.

la:noun:arbitrium.gloss: the decision of an arbiter, arbitration
senses: the decision of an arbiter, arbitration
discretion, liberal decision; arbitrary decision, whim
la:noun:arbitrium.html:
arbī^trĭum (in good MSS. and inscrr. sometimes arbī^tērĭum), ii, n.
from arbiter, as adulterium from adulter
.
In gen., a coming near, a being present, presence; hence meton. for persons present (only in post-Aug. poets): locus ab omni liber arbitrio. , and : divina rerum cura sine arbitrio est, Auct. Aetnae, 195.—
Esp.
The judgment, decision of an arbitrator (cf. arbiter, II.: arbitrium dicitur sententia, quae ab arbitro statuitur, Paul. ex Müll.): aliud est judicium, aliud arbitrium. Judicium est pecuniae certae: arbitrium incertae,: Q. Scaevola summam vim dicebat esse in omnibus iis arbitriis, in quibus adderetur ex fide bonā,; so, arbitrium rei uxoriae,; ; cf. ; fin.; : arbitrium pro socio condemnari solerent, B. and K. (here some consider arbitrium as a gloss, others read arbitrio, ad arbitrium, ad arbitrum, and the like; v. Orell. ad h. l.).—
Transf. from the sphere of judic. proceedings, judgment, opinion, decision: arbitrium vestrum, vestra existimatio Valebit,: cum de te splendida Minos Fecerit arbitria,: de aliquo arbitria agere,: arbitria belli pacisque agere,; cf. : agere arbitria victoriae,; cf. Gron. Observ. 4, c. 11, p. 427, and ; .— Trop.: res ab opinionis arbitrio sejunctae,matters, in which nothing is decided according to mere opinion,: si volet usus, Quem penes arbitrium est et jus et norma loquendi,; : arbitrio consilioque uti auris,to determine by the ear,.—
Mastery, dominion, authority, power, will, free-will: dedunt se In ditionem atque in arbitrium cuncti Thebano poplo, (Fleck., arbitratum): esse in pectore nostro quiddam, Cujus ad arbitrium quoque copia materiaiï Cogitur interdum flecti per membra, per artus, and at whose bidding the accumulated materials must yield obedience in every joint and limb, * : cujus (Jovis) nutu et arbitrio caelum, terra mariaque reguntur,: ad alicujus arbitrium et nutum totum se fingere et adcommodare,; ; fin.; so ; : aliquid facere arbitrio suo,: Mentes ad suum arbitrium movere,; so : quam (pecuniam) sponte et arbitrio cordis sui inferunt,: vixit ad aliorum arbitrium, non ad suum,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; ; : in arbitrium vestrum diem constituistis ei,: orationem tibi misi: ejus custodiendae et proferendae arbitrium tuum,: munificentiam eorum in se ipsorum arbitrii debere esse,: in arbitrio viri erit, ut faciat sive non faciat,: tamquam congruere operationem eam serpentium humani sit arbitrī,; ; : mox rei Romanae arbitrium (i. e. imperium, dominion, power) tribus ferme et viginti (annis) obtinuit, ; so, arbitrium orbis terrarum,; : huic deus optandi gratum, sed inutile fecit Muneris arbitrium,: liberum mortis arbitrium,; ; cf. .—
Arbitria funeris, the expenses of a funeral (fixed by an arbiter), ; ; ; cf. .

la:noun:arbustum.html:
arbustum, i, n.
qs. for arbosetum from arbos, as virgultum for virguletum, salictum for salicetum, etc.; an inferior form is arboretum, q. v.
,
a place where trees are planted (esp. trees, about which the vine was trained), an orchard, plantation, vineyard planted with trees, δενδρών (while vinea was one in which the vine lay upon the earth, or was supported by poles): Jam vinctae vites, jam falcem arbusta reponunt,.
Lit.: vinea est prima ... septimo silva caedua, octavo arbustum, nono glandaria silva,: In fundo suum quicquid conseri oportet arbustoque vitem copulari,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; —
Transf., for the most part in the plur. collect. for arbores, in the poets, on account of its quantity, ārbŏrēs: locos, Ingenio arbusta ubi nata sunt, non obsita, Naev. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 10 Rib.): e terrāque exorta repente arbusta salirent,trees springing up suddenly from the earth, shot forth,: florescunt tempore certo arbusta,trees blossom at the appointed time,; so ; ; ; 2, 188; 2, 1016; 5, 912; 5, 1378; 6, 141; ; ; ; 5, 64; ; id. Copa, 27; ; ; —So also perh. in the sing. for a single tree: cum me arbustum videre Miconis incidere falce,.—In the Vulg. only in plur., and there for rami, boughs, branches: arbusta ejus (vitis) cedros Dei, Psa. 79, 11: Multiplicata sunt arbusta ejus, Ezech. 31, 5; 31, 7; 31, 12.
